A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery
There Was a Bold Lady Who Wanted a Star
When I was little: A four-year-old's memoir of her youth.

pieces.name: Bilingual Education
pieces.about: In bilingual education, students are taught in two languages. It is distinct from learning a second language as a subject because both languages are used for instruction in different content areas like math, science, and history. The time spent in each language depends on the model. For example, some models focus on providing education in both languages throughout a student's entire education while others gradually transition to education in only one language. The ultimate goal of bilingual education is fluency and literacy in both languages through a variety of strategies such as translanguaging and recasting.

pieces.name: Black Market
pieces.about: A black market, underground economy, or shadow economy is a clandestine market or series of transactions that has some aspect of illegality or is not compliant with an institutional set of rules. If the rule defines the set of goods and services whose production and distribution is prohibited or restricted by law, non-compliance with the rule constitutes a black-market trade since the transaction itself is illegal. Such transactions include the illegal drug trade, prostitution, illegal currency transactions, and human trafficking.

pieces.name: Bracelet
pieces.about: A bracelet is an article of jewellery that is worn around the wrist. Bracelets may serve different uses, such as being worn as an ornament. When worn as ornaments, bracelets may have a supportive function to hold other items of decoration, such as charms. Medical and identity information are marked on some bracelets, such as allergy bracelets, hospital patient-identification tags, and bracelet tags for newborn babies. Bracelets may be worn to signify a certain phenomenon, such as breast cancer awareness, or for religious/cultural purposes.

also.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs

pieces.name: Brass knuckles
pieces.about: Brass knuckles are a melee weapon used primarily in hand-to-hand combat. They are fitted and designed to be worn around the knuckles of the human hand. Despite their name, they are often made from other metals, plastics or carbon fibers and not necessarily brass.

pieces.name: Bronchitis
pieces.about: Bronchitis - Symptoms and causes - Mayo Clinic

pieces.name: Buzz cut
pieces.about: A buzz cut, or wiffle cut, is a variety of short hairstyles, especially where the length of hair is the same on all parts of the head. Rising to prominence initially with the advent of manual hair clippers, buzz cuts became increasingly popular in places where strict grooming conventions applied. In several nations, buzz cuts are often given to new recruits in the armed forces or newly incarcerated inmates. However, buzz cuts are also used for stylistic reasons.

pieces.name: Camera
pieces.about: A camera is an instrument used to capture and store images and videos, either digitally via an electronic image sensor, or chemically via a light-sensitive material such as photographic film. As a pivotal technology in the fields of photography and videography, cameras have played a significant role in the progression of visual arts, media, entertainment, surveillance, and scientific research. The invention of the camera dates back to the 19th century and has since evolved with advancements in technology, leading to a vast array of types and models in the 21st century.

also.title: Born a Crime: Stories from a South African Childhood

pieces.name: Candied Apple
pieces.about: Candy apples are whole apples covered in a sugar candy coating, with a stick inserted as a handle. These are a common treat at fall festivals in Western culture in the Northern Hemisphere, such as Halloween and Guy Fawkes Night because these festivals occur in the wake of annual apple harvests. Although candy apples and caramel apples may seem similar, they are made using distinctly different processes.

pieces.name: Carpet Weaving
pieces.about: A Persian carpet or Persian rug, also known as Iranian carpet, is a heavy textile made for a wide variety of utilitarian and symbolic purposes and produced in Iran, for home use, local sale, and export. Carpet weaving is an essential part of Persian culture and Iranian art. Within the group of Oriental rugs produced by the countries of the "rug belt", the Persian carpet stands out by the variety and elaborateness of its manifold designs.

pieces.name: Chador
pieces.about: A chādor, also variously spelled in English as chadah, chad(d)ar, chader, chud(d)ah, chadur, and naturalized as, is an outer garment or open cloak worn by many women in the Persian-influenced countries of Iran, Afghanistan, Kashmir, Pakistan, and to a lesser extent Tajikistan, as well as in Shia communities in Iraq, Bahrain, and Qatif in Saudi Arabia in public spaces or outdoors.

pieces.name: Chemical weapon
pieces.about: A chemical weapon (CW) is a specialized munition that uses chemicals formulated to inflict death or harm on humans. According to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), this can be any chemical compound intended as a weapon "or its precursor that can cause death, injury, temporary incapacitation or sensory irritation through its chemical action. Munitions or other delivery devices designed to deliver chemical weapons, whether filled or unfilled, are also considered weapons themselves."

pieces.name: Chess
pieces.about: Chess is a board game for two players. It is sometimes called international chess or Western chess to distinguish it from related games such as xiangqi and shogi.

pieces.name: Church
pieces.about: A church, church building, or church house is a building used for Christian worship services and other Christian religious activities. The earliest identified Christian church is a house church founded between 233 and 256.

also.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs
John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads

pieces.name: Cigarette Butts
pieces.about: A cigarette is a narrow cylinder containing a combustible material, typically tobacco, that is rolled into thin paper for smoking. The cigarette is ignited at one end, causing it to smolder; the resulting smoke is orally inhaled via the opposite end. Cigarette smoking is the most common method of tobacco consumption. The term cigarette, as commonly used, refers to a tobacco cigarette, but the word is sometimes used to refer to other substances, such as a cannabis cigarette or a herbal cigarette. A cigarette is distinguished from a cigar by its usually smaller size, use of processed leaf, and paper wrapping, which is typically white.

pieces.about: (Page 204)

pieces.name: Culture (Iran)
pieces.about: The culture of Iran or culture of Persia is among the most influential in the world. Iran (Persia) is widely considered to be one of the cradles of civilization. Due to its dominant geopolitical position in the world, it has heavily influenced peoples and cultures situated as far away as Southern Europe and Eastern Europe to the west; Central Asia to the north; the Arabian Peninsula to the south; and South Asia, East Asia, and Southeast Asia to the east. Iranian history has had a significant influence on the world through art, architecture, poetry, science and technology, medicine, philosophy, and engineering.

pieces.name: Deck of Cards
pieces.about: A playing card is a piece of specially prepared card stock, heavy paper, thin cardboard, plastic-coated paper, cotton-paper blend, or thin plastic that is marked with distinguishing motifs. Often the front (face) and back of each card has a finish to make handling easier. They are most commonly used for playing card games, and are also used in magic tricks, cardistry, card throwing, and card houses; cards may also be collected. Playing cards are typically palm-sized for convenient handling, and usually are sold together in a set as a deck of cards or pack of cards.

pieces.name: Denim Jacket
pieces.about: A denim jacket, also called a jean jacket, jeans jacket or trucker jacket, is a jacket made from denim. Introduced in the United States in the late 19th century, it has been a popular type of casual apparel with both men and women and has been described as an iconic element of American fashion. Though a staple of western wear, the denim jacket has also enjoyed a more general appeal.

pieces.name: Dialectical Materialism (comic book)
pieces.about: Dialectical materialism is a materialist theory based upon the writings of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels that has found widespread applications in a variety of philosophical disciplines ranging from philosophy of history to philosophy of science. As a materialist philosophy, Marxist dialectics emphasizes the importance of real-world conditions and the presence of functional contradictions within and among social relations, which derive from, but are not limited to, the contradictions that occur in social class, labour economics, and socioeconomic interactions. Within Marxism, a contradiction is a relationship in which two forces oppose each other, leading to mutual development.

pieces.name: Dowry
pieces.about: A dowry is a payment, such as property or money, paid by the bride's family to the groom or his family at the time of marriage. Dowry contrasts with the related concepts of bride price and dower. While bride price or bride service is a payment by the groom, or his family, to the bride, or her family, dowry is the wealth transferred from the bride, or her family, to the groom, or his family. Similarly, dower is the property settled on the bride herself, by the groom at the time of marriage, and which remains under her ownership and control.

pieces.name: Earmuffs
pieces.about: Earmuffs are clothing accessories or personal protective equipment designed to cover a person's ears for hearing protection or warmth. They consist of a thermoplastic or metal head-band that fits over the top or back of the head, and a cushion or cup at each end to cover the ears.

pieces.name: Espadrille
pieces.about: Espadrilles are casual, rope-soled, flat but sometimes high-heeled shoes. They usually have a canvas or cotton fabric upper and a flexible sole made of esparto rope. The esparto rope sole is the defining characteristic of an espadrille; the uppers vary widely in style.

pieces.name: Eyeliner
pieces.about: Eye liner or eyeliner is a cosmetic used to define the eyes. It is applied around the contours of the eye(s). It is often used to create various aesthetic effects.

pieces.name: Eye of the Tiger (Song)
pieces.about: "Eye of the Tiger" is a song by the American rock band Survivor. It was written as the theme song for the 1982 film Rocky III and released that year as a single from Survivor's third album, Eye of the Tiger.

pieces.name: F14 Tomcat
pieces.about: The Grumman F-14 Tomcat is an American carrier-capable supersonic, twin-engine, two-seat, twin-tail, all-weather-capable variable-sweep wing fighter aircraft. The Tomcat was developed for the United States Navy's Naval Fighter Experimental (VFX) program after the collapse of the General Dynamics-Grumman F-111B project. A large and well-equipped fighter, the F-14 was the first of the American Teen Series fighters, which were designed incorporating air combat experience against MiG fighters during the Vietnam War.

pieces.name: Forest
pieces.about: A large area of land covered chiefly with trees and undergrowth.

pieces.name: Frankenstein
pieces.about: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus is an 1818 novel written by English author Mary Shelley. Frankenstein tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. Shelley started writing the story when she was 18, and the first edition was published anonymously in London on 1 January 1818, when she was 20. Her name first appeared in the second edition, which was published in Paris in 1821.

pieces.name: Hair Dryer
pieces.about: A hair dryer, hairdryer, hairdrier or blow dryer is an electromechanical device that blows ambient or hot air over damp hair to speed the evaporation of water to dry the hair. Blow dryers enable better control over the shape and style of hair, by accelerating and controlling the formation of temporary hydrogen bonds within each strand. These bonds are powerful but are temporary and extremely vulnerable to humidity. They disappear with a single washing of the hair.

pieces.name: Heidi
pieces.about: Heidi is a work of children's fiction published between 1880 and 1881 by Swiss author Johanna Spyri, originally published in two parts as Heidi: Her Years of Wandering and Learning and Heidi: How She Used What She Learned. It is a novel about the events in the life of a 5-year-old girl in her paternal grandfather's care in the Swiss Alps. It was written as a book "for children and those who love children".

pieces.name: Hijab
pieces.about: After the 1979 Iranian Revolution, it became compulsory for women to cover their hair in Iran with a scarf that covered the hair and neck, but not the face. Hijab was seen as a symbol of piety, dignity, and identity for Muslim women.

pieces.name: Inside the CIA (Book)
pieces.about: Examination of the CIA from the perspective of its prominent directors, veteran officers, and significant critics

pieces.name: Jasmin
pieces.about: Jasmine is a genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family of Oleaceae. It contains around 200 species native to tropical and warm temperate regions of Eurasia, Africa, and Oceania. Jasmines are widely cultivated for the characteristic fragrance of their flowers. Additionally a number of unrelated species of plants or flowers contain the word "jasmine" in their common names.

pieces.name: Jerrycan
pieces.about: A jerrycan or jerrican is a fuel container made from pressed steel. It was designed in Germany in the 1930s for military use to hold 20 litres of fuel, and saw widespread use by both Germany and the Allies during the Second World War.

pieces.name: Kids in America
pieces.about: "Kids in America" is a song recorded by English pop singer Kim Wilde. It was released in the United Kingdom as her debut single in January 1981, and in the United States in spring 1982, later appearing on her self-titled debut studio album. Largely inspired by the synth-pop style of Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (OMD) and Gary Numan, the song reached number two on the UK Singles Chart for two weeks and number one in Finland and South Africa, and charted in the top 10 of many European charts as well as Australia and New Zealand. In North America, the song reached the top 40 in Canada and the United States. It was certified gold in the United Kingdom, South Africa, Australia and Sweden; and has sold over three million copies worldwide. The song has been covered by many artists from different genres.

pieces.name: Kurdish
pieces.about: Kurdish is a Northwestern Iranian language or group of languages spoken by Kurds in the region of Kurdistan, namely in Turkey, northern Iraq, northwest and northeast Iran, and Syria.

pieces.name: La Dolce Vita
pieces.about: La dolce vita is a 1960 satirical comedy-drama film directed and co-written by Federico Fellini. The film stars Marcello Mastroianni as Marcello Rubini, a tabloid journalist who, over seven days and nights, journeys through the "sweet life" of Rome in a fruitless search for love and happiness. The screenplay, written by Fellini and three other screenwriters, can be divided into a prologue, seven major episodes interrupted by an intermezzo, and an epilogue, according to the most common interpretation.

pieces.name: La Pieta
pieces.about: The Madonna della Pietà, informally known as La Pietà, is a marble sculpture of Jesus and Mary at Mount Golgotha representing the "Sixth Sorrow" of the Blessed Virgin Mary by Michelangelo Buonarroti, now in Saint Peter's Basilica, Vatican City. It is a key work of Italian Renaissance sculpture and often taken as the start of the High Renaissance.

pieces.name: Lederhosen
pieces.about: The term Lederhosen is used in English to refer specifically to the traditional leather breeches worn by men in Austria, Bavaria, and South Tyrol. The term Trachten Lederhose is often used in German to avoid confusion with other types of leather pants.

pieces.name: Les Misérables (Book)
pieces.about: Les Misérables is a French historical novel by Victor Hugo, first published in 1862, that is considered one of the greatest novels of the 19th century. Les Misérables has been popularized through numerous adaptations for film, television and the stage, including a musical.

pieces.name: Lipstick
pieces.about: Lipstick is a cosmetic product used to apply coloration and texture to lips, often made of wax and oil. Different pigments are used to produce color, and minerals such as silica may be used to provide texture. The use of lipstick dates back to early civilizations such as Sumer and the Indus Valley Civilisation, and was popularized in the Western world in the 16th century. Some lipsticks contain traces of toxic materials, such as lead and PFAS, which prompted health concerns and regulation.

pieces.name: Mein Kampf (Book)
pieces.about: Mein Kampf is a 1925 autobiographical manifesto by Nazi Party leader Adolf Hitler. The work describes the process by which Hitler became antisemitic and outlines his political ideology and future plans for Germany. Volume 1 of Mein Kampf was published in 1925 and Volume 2 in 1926. The book was edited first by Emil Maurice, then by Hitler's deputy Rudolf Hess.

pieces.name: Mig 29
pieces.about: The Mikoyan MiG-29 is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union. Developed by the Mikoyan design bureau as an air superiority fighter during the 1970s, the MiG-29, along with the larger Sukhoi Su-27, was developed to counter new U.S. fighters such as the McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle and the General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon. The MiG-29 entered service with the Soviet Air Forces in 1983.

pieces.name: Monopoly (board game)
pieces.about: Monopoly is a multiplayer economics-themed board game. In the game, players roll two dice to move around the game board, buying and trading properties and developing them with houses and hotels. Players collect rent from their opponents and aim to drive them into bankruptcy. Money can also be gained or lost through Chance and Community Chest cards and tax squares. Players receive a salary every time they pass "Go" and can end up in jail, from which they cannot move until they have met one of three conditions. House rules, hundreds of different editions, many spin-offs, and related media exist. Monopoly has become a part of international popular culture, having been licensed locally in more than 103 countries and printed in more than 37 languages. As of 2015, it was estimated that the game had sold 275 million copies worldwide. The original game was based on locations in Atlantic City, New Jersey, United States with the exception of Marven Gardens which is in adjacent Ventnor, NJ.

pieces.name: Mosque
pieces.about: A mosque, also called a masjid, is a place of worship for Muslims. The term usually refers to a covered building, but can be any place where Islamic prayers are performed, such as an outdoor courtyard.

pieces.name: Oil
pieces.about: Petroleum or crude oil, also referred to as simply oil, is a naturally occurring yellowish-black liquid mixture of mainly hydrocarbons, and is found in geological formations. The name petroleum covers both naturally occurring unprocessed crude oil and petroleum products that consist of refined crude oil.

pieces.name: Oshin
pieces.about: Oshin (おしん) is a Japanese serialized morning television drama (asadora), which originally aired on NHK from 4 April 1983 to 31 March 1984; it is the 31st asadora overall to be produced. The 297 15-minute episodes follow the life of Shin Tanokura  during the Meiji period up to the early 1980s. In the work, Shin is called Oshin, the O- forming an archaic cognomen.

pieces.name: Passport
pieces.about: A passport is an official travel document issued by a government that contains a person's identity for international travel. A person with a passport can travel to and from foreign countries more easily and access consular assistance. A passport certifies the personal identity and nationality of its holder. It is typical for passports to contain the full name, photograph, place and date Apurba Senapati of birth 28/12/2005, signature, and the issue and expiration dates of the passport. While passports are typically issued by national governments, certain subnational governments are authorized to issue passports to citizens residing within their borders.

pieces.name: Persepolis (Book)
pieces.about: Persepolis is a series of autobiographical graphic novels by Marjane Satrapi that depict her childhood and early adult years in Iran and Austria during and after the Islamic Revolution. The title Persepolis is a reference to the ancient capital of the Persian Empire. Originally published in French, Persepolis has been translated to many other languages. As of 2018, it has sold more than 2 million copies worldwide.

pieces.name: Persian Culture
pieces.about: The culture of Iran or culture of Persia is among the most influential in the world. Iran (Persia) is widely considered to be one of the cradles of civilization. Due to its dominant geopolitical position in the world, it has heavily influenced peoples and cultures situated as far away as Southern Europe and Eastern Europe to the west; Central Asia to the north; the Arabian Peninsula to the south; and South Asia, East Asia, and Southeast Asia to the east. Iranian history has had a significant influence on the world through art, architecture, poetry, science and technology, medicine, philosophy, and engineering.

pieces.name: Persian Language
pieces.about: Persian, also known by its endonym Farsi or Parsi, is a Western Iranian language belonging to the Iranian branch of the Indo-Iranian subdivision of the Indo-European languages. Persian is a pluricentric language predominantly spoken and used officially within Iran, Afghanistan, and Tajikistan in three mutually intelligible standard varieties, respectively Iranian Persian, Dari Persian, and Tajiki Persian. It is also spoken natively in the Tajik variety by a significant population within Uzbekistan, as well as within other regions with a Persianate history in the cultural sphere of Greater Iran. It is written officially within Iran and Afghanistan in the Persian alphabet, a derivative of the Arabic script, and within Tajikistan in the Tajik alphabet, a derivative of the Cyrillic script.

pieces.name: Picture frame
pieces.about: A picture frame is a protective and decorative edging for a picture, such as a painting or photograph. It makes displaying the work safer and easier and both sets the picture apart from its surroundings and aesthetically integrates it with them.

pieces.name: Pistachio
pieces.about: The pistachio, a member of the cashew family, is a small tree originating in Persia. The tree produces seeds that are widely consumed as food. The word can be countable or uncountable, meaning its plural is with or without an 's'.

pieces.name: Refinery
pieces.about: An oil refinery or petroleum refinery is an industrial process plant where petroleum is transformed and refined into products such as gasoline (petrol), diesel fuel, asphalt base, fuel oils, heating oil, kerosene, liquefied petroleum gas and petroleum naphtha. Petrochemical feedstock like ethylene and propylene can also be produced directly by cracking crude oil without the need of using refined products of crude oil such as naphtha. The crude oil feedstock has typically been processed by an oil production plant. There is usually an oil depot at or near an oil refinery for the storage of incoming crude oil feedstock as well as bulk liquid products. In 2020, the total capacity of global refineries for crude oil was about 101.2 million barrels per day.

pieces.name: Rheumatism
pieces.about: Rheumatism or rheumatic disorders are conditions causing chronic, often intermittent pain affecting the joints or connective tissue. Rheumatism does not designate any specific disorder, but covers at least 200 different conditions, including arthritis and "non-articular rheumatism", also known as "regional pain syndrome" or "soft tissue rheumatism". There is a close overlap between the term soft tissue disorder and rheumatism. Sometimes the term "soft tissue rheumatic disorders" is used to describe these conditions.

pieces.name: Sachertorte
pieces.about: Sachertorte is a chocolate cake, or torte, of Austrian origin, invented by Franz Sacher, supposedly in 1832 for Prince Metternich in Vienna. It is one of the most famous Viennese culinary specialties.

pieces.name: Samovar
pieces.about: A samovar is a metal container traditionally used to heat and boil water. Although originating in Russia, the samovar is well known outside of Russia and has spread through Russian culture to other parts of Eastern Europe, as well as Western and Central and South Asia. Since the heated water is typically used to make tea, many samovars have a ring-shaped attachment around the chimney to hold and heat a teapot filled with tea concentrate. Though traditionally heated with coal or kindling, many newer samovars use electricity to heat water in a manner similar to an electric water boiler. Antique samovars are often prized for their beautiful workmanship.

pieces.name: Satellite Antenna
pieces.about: Satellite television is a service that delivers television programming to viewers by relaying it from a communications satellite orbiting the Earth directly to the viewer's location. The signals are received via an outdoor parabolic antenna commonly referred to as a satellite dish and a low-noise block downconverter.

pieces.name: Scented Pens
pieces.about: Mr. Sketch is a brand of scented markers, currently owned by Newell Brands. Its markers are sold in packages of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 18 and 22 units. Mr. Sketch markers come in both chisel and fine point. The markers have large strokes and can be used for posters and group work. Mr. Sketch markers have many different colors to choose from.

pieces.name: Scud missile
pieces.about: A Scud missile is one of a series of tactical ballistic missiles developed by the Soviet Union during the Cold War. It was exported widely to both Second and Third World countries. The term comes from the NATO reporting name attached to the missile by Western intelligence agencies. The Russian names for the missile are the R-11, and the R-17 Elbrus. The name Scud has been widely used to refer to these missiles and the wide variety of derivative variants developed in other countries based on the Soviet design.

pieces.name: Shish_kebab
pieces.about: Shish kebab or shish kebap is a popular meal of skewered and grilled cubes of meat. It can be found in Mediterranean cuisine and it may come from a dish called souvlaki, found in Greek cuisine.

pieces.name: Sissi (Movie)
pieces.about: Sissi is a 1955 Austrian historical romance film written and directed by Ernst Marischka and starring Romy Schneider, Karlheinz Böhm, Magda Schneider, Uta Franz, Gustav Knuth, Josef Meinrad, Vilma Degischer and Peter Weck. Sissi is the first installment in the trilogy of films about Empress Elisabeth of Austria, who was known to her family as "Sisi". It was followed by The Young Empress and Fateful Years of an Empress.

pieces.name: Ski Suit
pieces.about: A ski suit is a suit made to be worn over the rest of the clothes when skiing or snowboarding. A ski suit made for more casual winter wear outdoors may also be called a snowsuit [ˈsnoʊˌsut] and are often used by children as everyday outerwear in the winter season. Some suits are specifically made for snowboarders but most are used by either skiers or snowboarders regardless of the style.

pieces.name: Star Wars (Movie)
pieces.about: Star Wars is an American epic space opera media franchise created by George Lucas, which began with the eponymous 1977 film and quickly became a worldwide pop culture phenomenon. The franchise has been expanded into various films and other media, including television series, video games, novels, comic books, theme park attractions, and themed areas, comprising an all-encompassing fictional universe. Star Wars is one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time.

pieces.name: The Mandarins (Book)
pieces.about: The Mandarins is a 1954 roman à clef by Simone de Beauvoir, for which she won the Prix Goncourt, awarded to the best and most imaginative prose work of the year, in 1954. The Mandarins was first published in English in 1956.

pieces.name: The Picture of Dorian Gray (Book)
pieces.about: The Picture of Dorian Gray is a philosophical novel by Irish writer Oscar Wilde. A shorter novella-length version was published in the July 1890 issue of the American periodical Lippincott's Monthly Magazine. The novel-length version was published in April 1891.

pieces.name: Toman
pieces.about: The Iranian toman is a superunit of the official currency of Iran, the rial. One toman is equivalent to 10 (old), or 10,000 rials.

pieces.name: Tram (streetcar)
pieces.about: A tram is a type of urban rail transit consisting of a rail vehicle, either individual railcars or self-propelled trains coupled by a multiple unit, that runs on tramway tracks on urban public streets; some include segments on segregated right-of-way. The tramlines or networks operated as public transport are called tramways or simply trams/streetcars. Many recently built tramways use the contemporary term light rail.

pieces.name: Transcendental Meditation
pieces.about: Transcendental Meditation (TM) is a form of silent meditation developed by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and so named to separate it from Hinduism or any other religious practice. The TM technique involves the silent repetition of a mantra or sound, and is practiced for 15–20 minutes twice per day. It is taught by certified teachers through a standard course of instruction, which costs a fee that varies by country. According to the Transcendental Meditation movement, it is a non-religious method that promotes relaxed awareness, stress relief, self-development, and higher states of consciousness. The technique has been variously described as both religious and non-religious.

pieces.name: Trash can (Waste bin)
pieces.about: A waste container, also known as a dustbin, rubbish bin, trash can, and garbage can, among other names, is a type of container intended to store waste that is usually made out of metal or plastic. The words "rubbish", "basket" and "bin" are more common in British English usage; "trash" and "can" are more common in American English usage. "Garbage" may refer to food waste specifically or to municipal solid waste in general.

pieces.name: University Entrance Exam (Iran)
pieces.about: The Iranian University Entrance Exam, simply known as Konkour, is a standardized test used as one of the means to gain admission to higher education in Iran. Generally, to get a Ph.D. in non-medical majors, there are three exams, all of them called Konkour.

pieces.name: Veil
pieces.about: A veil is an article of clothing or hanging cloth that is intended to cover some part of the head or face, or an object of some significance. Veiling has a long history in European, Asian, and African societies. The practice has been prominent in different forms in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The practice of veiling is especially associated with women and sacred objects, though in some cultures, it is men, rather than women, who are expected to wear a veil. Besides its enduring religious significance, veiling continues to play a role in some modern secular contexts, such as wedding customs.

pieces.name: Video Cassette (VHS)
pieces.about: The VHS is a standard for consumer-level analog video recording on tape cassettes, invented in 1976 by the Victor Company of Japan (JVC). It was the dominant home video format throughout the tape media period in the 1980s and 1990s.

pieces.name: Vinyl Records
pieces.about: The LP is an analog sound storage medium, specifically a phonograph record format characterized by: a speed of 33+1⁄3 rpm; a 12- or 10-inch diameter; use of the "microgroove" groove specification; and a vinyl composition disk. Introduced by Columbia Records in 1948, it was soon adopted as a new standard by the entire US record industry and, apart from a few relatively minor refinements and the important later addition of stereophonic sound in 1957, it remained the standard format for record albums, during a period in popular music known as the album era. LP was originally a trademark of Columbia and competed against the smaller 7-inch sized "45" or "single" format by RCA Victor, eventually ending up on top. Today in the vinyl revival era, a large majority of records are based on the LP format and hence the LP name continues to be in use today to refer to new records.

pieces.name: Walkman
pieces.about: Walkman , is a brand of portable audio players manufactured and marketed by Japanese company Sony since 1979. The original Walkman started out as a portable cassette player and the brand was later extended to serve most of Sony's portable audio devices; since 2011 it consists exclusively of digital flash memory players. The current flagship product as of 2022 is the WM1ZM2 player.

pieces.name: Zarb/Tombak
pieces.about: The tombak, tonbak (تنبک) or zarb (ضَرب) is an Iranian goblet drum. It is considered the principal percussion instrument of Persian music. The tombak is normally positioned diagonally across the torso, while the player uses one or more fingers and/or the palm(s) of the hand(s) on the drumhead, often near the drumhead's edge. Sometimes, tombak players wear metal finger rings for an extra-percussive "click" on the drum's shell. Tombak virtuosi often perform solos lasting ten minutes or more.

pieces.name: 1953 coup d'état (Iran)
pieces.about: The 1953 Iranian coup d'état, known in Iran as the 28 Mordad coup d'état, was the U.S.- and British-instigated, Iranian army-led overthrow of the elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh in favor of strengthening the monarchical rule of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, on 19 August 1953, with one of the significant objectives being to protect British oil interests in Iran. It was aided by the United States and the United Kingdom.

pieces.name: Black Friday
pieces.about: Black Friday is the name given to an incident occurring on 8 September 1978 in Iran, in which 64, or at least 100 people were shot dead and 205 injured by the Pahlavi military in Jaleh Square in Tehran. According to the military historian Spencer C. Tucker, 94 were killed on Black Friday, consisting of 64 protesters and 30 government security forces. The deaths were described as the pivotal event in the Iranian Revolution that ended any "hope for compromise" between the protest movement and the regime of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

pieces.name: Iran Iraq War
pieces.about: The Iran–Iraq War, also known as the First Gulf War, was an armed conflict between Iran and Iraq that lasted from September 1980 to August 1988. Active hostilities began with the Iraqi invasion of Iran and lasted for eight years, until the acceptance of United Nations Security Council Resolution 598 by both sides. Iraq's primary rationale for the attack against Iran cited the need to prevent Ruhollah Khomeini—who had spearheaded the Iranian Revolution in 1979—from exporting the new Iranian ideology to Iraq. There were also fears among the Iraqi leadership of Saddam Hussein that Iran, a theocratic state with a population predominantly composed of Shia Muslims, would exploit sectarian tensions in Iraq by rallying Iraq's Shia majority against the Baʽathist government, which was officially secular and dominated by Sunni Muslims. Iraq also wished to replace Iran as the power player in the Persian Gulf, which was not seen as an achievable objective prior to the Islamic Revolution because of Pahlavi Iran's economic and military superiority as well as its close relationships with the United States and Israel.

pieces.name: Iraq Kuwait War (Persian Gulf War)
pieces.about: The Iraqi invasion of Kuwait began on 2 August 1990 and marked the beginning of the Gulf War. After defeating the State of Kuwait on 4 August 1990, Iraq went on to militarily occupy the country for the next seven months. The invasion was condemned internationally, and the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) adopted numerous resolutions urging Iraq to withdraw from Kuwaiti territory. The Iraqi military, however, continued to occupy Kuwait and defied all orders by the UNSC. After initially establishing the "Republic of Kuwait" as a puppet state, Iraq annexed the entire country on 28 August 1990; northern Kuwait became the Saddamiyat al-Mitla' District and was merged into the existing Basra Governorate, while southern Kuwait was carved out as the all-new Kuwait Governorate. By November 1990, the adoption of UNSC Resolution 678 officially issued Iraq an ultimatum to withdraw unconditionally by 15 January 1991 or else be removed by "all necessary means" from Kuwaiti territory. In anticipation of a war with Iraq, the UNSC authorized the assembly of an American-led military coalition.

pieces.name: Islamic Revolution
pieces.about: The Iranian Revolution, also known as the Islamic Revolution, was a series of events that culminated in the overthrow of the Pahlavi dynasty in 1979. The revolution also led to the replacement of the Imperial State of Iran by the present-day Islamic Republic of Iran, as the monarchical government of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was superseded by the theocratic government of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a religious cleric who had headed one of the rebel factions. The ousting of Pahlavi, the last Shah of Iran, formally marked the end of Iran's historical monarchy.

pieces.name: Midnight Mass
pieces.about: In many Western Christian traditions, Midnight Mass is the first liturgy of Christmastide that is celebrated on the night of Christmas Eve, traditionally beginning at midnight when Christmas Eve gives way to Christmas Day. This popular Christmas custom is a jubilant celebration of the mass or service of worship in honour of the Nativity of Jesus; even many of those Christian denominations that do not regularly employ the word mass uniquely use the term "Midnight Mass" for their Christmas Eve liturgy as it includes the celebration of Holy Communion.

pieces.name: Mongol invasion of Persia
pieces.about: The Mongol conquest of Persia comprised three Mongol campaigns against Islamic states in the Middle East and Central Asia between 1219 and 1258. These campaigns led to the termination of the Khwarazmian dynasty, the Nizari Ismaili state, and the Abbasid Caliphate of Baghdad, and the establishment of the Mongol Ilkhanate government in their place in Persia.

pieces.name: Muslim Conquest of Persia
pieces.about: The Muslim conquest of Persia, also called the Muslim conquest of Iran, the Arab conquest of Persia, or the Arab conquest of Iran, was a major military campaign undertaken by the Rashidun Caliphate between 632 and 654. As part of the early Muslim conquests, which had begun under Muhammad in 622, it led to the fall of the Sasanian Empire and the eventual decline of Zoroastrianism, which had been predominant throughout Persia as the nation's official religion. The persecution of Zoroastrians by the early Muslims during and after this conflict prompted many of them to flee eastward to India, where they were granted refuge by various kings.

pieces.name: Nowruz
pieces.about: Nowruz or Navroz is the Iranian New Year or Persian New Year. Historically, it has been observed by Persians and other Iranian peoples, but is now celebrated by many ethnicities worldwide. It is a festival based on the Northern Hemisphere spring equinox, which marks the first day of a new year on the Solar Hijri calendar; it usually coincides with a date between 19 March and 22 March on the Gregorian calendar.

pieces.name: Rex Cinema Fire
pieces.about: The Cinema Rex fire happened on 19 August 1978 when the Cinema Rex in Abadan, Iran was set ablaze, killing between 377 and 470 people. The event started when four individuals, who were militants motivated by Islamic extremism, doused the building with airplane fuel before setting it alight. The attack was responsible in part for triggering the Iranian Revolution of 1979, which saw the overthrow of the ruling dynasty under the Iranian monarch and a related outbreak of mass violence. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in history until the 1990 massacre of Sri Lankan Police officers.

pieces.name: Sabbath (Shabbat)
pieces.about: In Abrahamic religions, the Sabbath or Shabbat is a day set aside for rest and worship. According to the Book of Exodus, the Sabbath is a day of rest on the seventh day, commanded by God to be kept as a holy day of rest, as God rested from creation. The practice of observing the Sabbath (Shabbat) originates in the biblical commandment "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy".

pieces.name: Vietnam War
pieces.about: The Vietnam War was a conflict in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia from 1 November 1955 to the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975. It was the second of the Indochina Wars and was a major conflict of the Cold War. While the war was officially fought between North Vietnam and South Vietnam, the north was supported by the Soviet Union, China, and other communist states, while the south was supported by the United States and other anti-communist allies, making the war a proxy war between the United States and the Soviet Union. It lasted almost 20 years, with direct U.S. military involvement ending in 1973. The conflict also spilled over into neighboring states, exacerbating the Laotian Civil War and the Cambodian Civil War, which ended with all three countries officially becoming communist states by 1976.

pieces.name: World War II
pieces.about: World War II or the Second World War was a global conflict between two alliances: the Allies and the Axis powers. Nearly all of the world's countries, including all of the great powers, participated in the conflict, and many invested all available economic, industrial, and scientific capabilities in pursuit of total war, blurring the distinction between civilian and military resources. Aircraft played a major role, enabling the strategic bombing of population centres and delivery of the only two nuclear weapons ever used in war. It was by far the deadliest conflict in history, resulting in 70–85 million fatalities. Millions died due to genocides, including the Holocaust, as well as starvation, massacres, and disease. In the wake of Axis defeat, Germany, Austria, and Japan were occupied, and war crime tribunals were conducted against German and Japanese leaders.

pieces.name: Anarchism
pieces.about: Anarchism is a political philosophy and movement that advocates for the abolition of hierarchical structures, including governments, and envisions a society based on voluntary cooperation, mutual aid, and individual autonomy. Anarchists seek to create a stateless, non-coercive society where individuals are free to organize and govern themselves collectively, without centralized authority. Anarchism opposes all forms of domination and oppression, including capitalism, statism, and other systems that limit individual freedom and perpetuate inequality.

pieces.name: Arson
pieces.about: Arson is the criminal act of intentionally setting fire to property, buildings, or structures with the intent to cause damage, destruction, or harm. It is typically done for malicious or unlawful purposes, such as insurance fraud, revenge, vandalism, or to conceal another crime.  Arson poses significant risks to public safety and property, and efforts to prevent and investigate arson are essential for maintaining community safety and security.

pieces.name: Art Education
pieces.about: Art education refers to the process of teaching and learning about visual arts, including various forms such as drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, photography, and digital media. It encompasses both the practice of creating art and the study of art history, theory, and criticism. Art education aims to develop students' creativity, critical thinking, aesthetic appreciation, and technical skills, while also fostering cultural awareness, self-expression, and personal growth. It may be offered at various levels of education, including primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, as well as through community programs, museums, and cultural institutions. Art education plays a crucial role in promoting artistic literacy, cultural enrichment, and the development of well-rounded individuals capable of engaging with and contributing to the arts and society.

pieces.name: Assimilation
pieces.about: Assimilation is the process by which individuals or groups adopt the cultural norms, values, and practices of another culture, often resulting in a loss of distinct identity or heritage. It involves integrating into the dominant culture and adopting its language, customs, beliefs, and behaviors, while relinquishing or modifying aspects of one's own culture. Assimilation can occur voluntarily as individuals seek to adapt to a new environment or community, or it can be enforced through social pressure, discrimination, or government policies. Assimilation can lead to social cohesion and integration but may also involve challenges such as identity conflict, loss of cultural heritage, and marginalization.

pieces.name: Breaking the Law
pieces.about: Breaking the law refers to the act of violating established legal statutes, regulations, or codes of conduct set forth by a governing authority. This can encompass a wide range of actions, from minor infractions such as traffic violations or petty theft to more serious offenses including assault, fraud, or homicide. Breaking the law can result in legal consequences such as fines, penalties, imprisonment, or other forms of punishment, depending on the severity of the offense and the jurisdiction in which it occurs. It undermines social order, threatens public safety, and erodes trust in the legal system, making adherence to the law essential for maintaining a just and orderly society.

pieces.name: Censorship (Iran)
pieces.about: Censorship in Iran refers to the systematic suppression or control of information, expression, and media content by the Iranian government and authorities. It involves various mechanisms and regulations aimed at restricting or manipulating the flow of information to align with government policies, ideologies, and religious principles.

pieces.name: Christmas (Winter) Break
pieces.about: Christmas break, also known as winter break or holiday break, is a period of time typically observed by schools, colleges, and universities around the Christmas holiday. It usually begins a few days before Christmas Day and extends through New Year's Day or into early January. During Christmas break, students and educators are often granted time off from classes and academic responsibilities to celebrate the holiday season with their families and loved ones. It provides an opportunity for rest, relaxation, and festivities, as well as travel and vacation activities. Christmas break varies in duration depending on the educational institution and local customs, but it generally allows students and staff to recharge and enjoy the holiday season before returning to their academic pursuits.

pieces.name: Communism
pieces.about: Communism is a socio-economic and political ideology that advocates for the establishment of a classless, stateless society where the means of production are commonly owned and controlled by the community as a whole. It emerged as a response to the inequalities and exploitation of capitalist systems.

pieces.name: Dating
pieces.about: Dating refers to the social activity and romantic relationship between two people who spend time together, usually with the intention of assessing their compatibility for a potential long-term partnership or marriage. It involves various interactions, such as going on dates, spending time together, and getting to know each other on a personal and emotional level. Dating can encompass a range of activities, from casual outings and dinners to more formal events and shared experiences. It often involves mutual attraction, emotional connection, and the exploration of shared interests, values, and goals. While the specific customs and norms of dating may vary across cultures and societies, the underlying goal is typically to establish a romantic connection and build a meaningful relationship.

pieces.name: Demonstration
pieces.about: A demonstration is a public gathering or protest where individuals come together to express their opinions, grievances, or demands on a particular issue or cause. Demonstrations can take various forms, ranging from peaceful marches and rallies to sit-ins, strikes, and civil disobedience.

pieces.name: Depression
pieces.about: Depression is a mental health disorder characterized by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and a loss of interest or pleasure in activities that were once enjoyable. It can also involve changes in appetite or weight, sleep disturbances, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, difficulty concentrating, and thoughts of death or suicide. Depression can vary in severity and duration, ranging from mild and temporary episodes to chronic and debilitating conditions. It can significantly impair daily functioning, relationships, and overall quality of life. Depression is a common and treatable condition, often requiring a combination of therapy, medication, lifestyle changes, and support from healthcare professionals and loved ones.

pieces.name: Divorce
pieces.about: Divorce is the legal dissolution or termination of a marriage or marital union, resulting in the formal severance of the marital relationship between spouses. It involves the legal process by which a court or other authority grants a decree or judgment ending the marital bond, thereby allowing the parties to remarry or enter into new relationships. Divorce can be initiated by one or both spouses and typically involves the resolution of issues such as division of property, child custody, visitation rights, and financial support. It represents the end of a marital partnership and can have significant emotional, social, and financial implications for the individuals involved and any children of the marriage.

pieces.name: Dress code
pieces.about: A dress code is a set of guidelines or rules that specify the acceptable attire and appearance for a particular situation, event, or environment. It defines the expectations for clothing, grooming, and personal presentation, often based on factors such as the context, formality, and cultural norms. Dress codes can vary widely depending on the setting, ranging from formal attire required for events such as weddings or business meetings to casual dress appropriate for everyday activities. They may be established by organizations, institutions, workplaces, schools, or social groups to promote professionalism, maintain decorum, ensure safety, or reflect cultural or religious values. Dress codes help establish a standard of dress and behavior, shaping perceptions, interactions, and social dynamics within a given context.

pieces.name: Drugs
pieces.about: Drugs are substances that alter the functioning of the body and mind when consumed. They can be classified into various categories, including pharmaceutical drugs used for medical purposes, recreational drugs taken for pleasure or euphoria, and illicit drugs that are prohibited by law. Drugs can have both beneficial and harmful effects on individuals, depending on factors such as dosage, frequency of use, and individual characteristics.

pieces.name: Emotional Support
pieces.about: Emotional support refers to the provision of comfort, empathy, understanding, and encouragement to someone who is experiencing emotional distress, difficulties, or challenges. It involves offering a compassionate presence, listening attentively, and validating the feelings and experiences of the individual in need. Emotional support can be provided by friends, family members, peers, or professionals, and it plays a crucial role in promoting mental and emotional well-being. It helps individuals feel heard, valued, and supported during times of crisis, grief, stress, or uncertainty, contributing to resilience, coping, and healing.

pieces.name: Escaping Iran After the Revolution
pieces.about: Escaping Iran after the revolution was a harrowing experience for many Iranians who sought to flee the political turmoil, repression, and economic hardship that followed the 1979 Islamic Revolution. The revolution led to the establishment of an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini, which implemented strict Islamic laws and cracked down on dissent.

pieces.name: False Impressions
pieces.about: False impressions refer to incorrect or misleading perceptions, beliefs, or understandings formed about someone or something due to incomplete, inaccurate, or deceptive information. These impressions can arise from various sources, including miscommunication, biased interpretations, manipulation, or lack of context. False impressions may lead to misunderstandings, misjudgments, and flawed decision-making, as they do not accurately reflect reality or the true nature of the person, situation, or thing being perceived.

pieces.name: Family History
pieces.about: Family history refers to the record or narrative of an individual's ancestors, relatives, and familial lineage over generations. It typically includes information about family members' names, dates of birth and death, relationships, occupations, residences, and significant life events such as marriages, births, and migrations. Family history can also encompass stories, traditions, and cultural heritage passed down through oral history or written records. Studying and documenting family history can provide insights into one's genealogy, heritage, and identity, as well as connections to broader historical events and social contexts. It allows individuals to understand their roots, preserve their family legacy, and connect with relatives across generations.

pieces.name: Fanaticism
pieces.about: An extreme and often irrational enthusiasm, devotion, or zeal for a particular belief, ideology, or cause. It involves an uncompromising and fervent commitment to one's beliefs, sometimes to the point of intolerance or violence towards those who hold differing views. Fanaticism can manifest in various contexts, including religion, politics, sports, or social causes, and it often disregards rationality and reason in pursuit of its objectives. (Intro)

pieces.name: Fear
pieces.about: Fear is an intense emotional response to a perceived threat, danger, or harm. It triggers physiological and psychological reactions, including increased heart rate, sweating, trembling, and heightened alertness. Fear serves as a natural survival mechanism, preparing individuals to react to potential dangers by either confronting the threat or fleeing from it. However, excessive or irrational fear can lead to anxiety, avoidance behaviors, and impairments in daily functioning. Fear can arise from various sources, including real threats, imagined dangers, past traumas, and cultural influences.

pieces.name: Forgery
pieces.about: Forgery is the act of creating, altering, or imitating a document, signature, artwork, or other item with the intent to deceive or defraud others. It involves producing a fraudulent copy or imitation that appears genuine and authentic, often for the purpose of gaining financial, legal, or personal advantage. Forgery can take various forms, including counterfeiting currency, falsifying signatures on contracts or checks, replicating artworks or collectibles, or fabricating official documents such as IDs or passports. Forgery is illegal and punishable by law, as it undermines trust, integrity, and the reliability of documents and institutions.

pieces.name: Friendship

pieces.name: Fundamentalism
pieces.about: A strict adherence to traditional beliefs, values, or doctrines, often within a religious or ideological context. It typically involves a literal interpretation of sacred texts or principles and a resistance to change or modernization. Fundamentalist movements can be found in various religions and ideologies, and they often advocate for a return to what they perceive as the fundamental or original principles of their faith or ideology. pieces.name: Greek Mythology
pieces.about: Greek mythology is a collection of stories, legends, and myths originating from ancient Greece. These myths are rich in gods, goddesses, heroes, monsters, and other supernatural beings, and they serve to explain natural phenomena, cultural practices, and the origins of the world. Greek mythology provides valuable insights into ancient Greek society, beliefs, and values, while also captivating audiences with its timeless tales of gods, heroes, and monsters.

pieces.name: Group Therapy
pieces.about: Group therapy is a form of psychotherapy where a small group of individuals meets regularly with a trained therapist to discuss and explore their emotions, experiences, and interpersonal relationships in a supportive and confidential environment. The group setting allows participants to share their concerns, receive feedback, and offer support to one another. Group therapy can be beneficial for addressing a wide range of psychological issues, including depression, anxiety, addiction, trauma, and relationship problems. It offers opportunities for social interaction, empathy, and mutual understanding, while also providing a sense of belonging and validation. Group therapy sessions are typically structured and guided by the therapist, who facilitates discussion, encourages collaboration, and promotes personal growth and self-awareness among group members.

pieces.name: Growth Mindset
pieces.about: A growth mindset is a belief or attitude that emphasizes the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, persistence, and learning. Individuals with a growth mindset perceive challenges, setbacks, and failures as opportunities for growth and improvement, rather than fixed limitations on their abilities. They embrace challenges, seek feedback, and are resilient in the face of obstacles, viewing failures as valuable learning experiences. A growth mindset fosters motivation, resilience, and a willingness to take on new challenges, ultimately leading to higher levels of achievement and personal development.

pieces.name: Heritage
pieces.about: Heritage refers to the collective legacy, traditions, values, beliefs, customs, and artifacts passed down from generation to generation within a particular community, society, or culture. It encompasses tangible and intangible aspects of culture, including historical sites, landmarks, monuments, artifacts, languages, rituals, music, cuisine, literature, and oral traditions. Heritage reflects the shared identity and experiences of a group of people and contributes to their sense of belonging, cultural identity, and continuity over time. Preserving and celebrating heritage is essential for understanding and appreciating the diversity and richness of human cultures, fostering social cohesion, and transmitting knowledge and values to future generations.

pieces.name: Homelessness
pieces.about: Homelessness is a state of living in which individuals or families lack stable, safe, and adequate housing, often resulting in living on the streets, in shelters, or in temporary accommodations. Homelessness can be caused by various factors, including poverty, unemployment, housing shortages, mental illness, substance abuse, domestic violence, and social or economic crises. It is a complex and multifaceted issue that affects individuals of all ages, backgrounds, and circumstances. Homelessness can have profound impacts on physical and mental health, as well as on overall well-being and quality of life. Efforts to address homelessness typically involve providing access to affordable housing, supportive services, employment assistance, and community resources.

pieces.name: Human Rights
pieces.about: A right that is believed to belong justifiably to every person regardless of nationality, sex, national or ethnic origin, color, religion, language, or any other status.

pieces.name: Illegal Border Crossing
pieces.about: Illegal border crossing refers to the act of crossing international borders without authorization or proper documentation from relevant authorities. This typically involves circumventing immigration checkpoints, border patrols, and other security measures put in place to regulate the movement of people across national boundaries. (Page 66)

pieces.name: Independent Living
pieces.about: Independent living refers to the ability of an individual to manage their own life and make decisions without relying on others for assistance or support. For someone leaving home, independent living involves taking responsibility for various aspects of daily life, including housing, finances, personal care, and household tasks. It entails developing skills such as budgeting, cooking, cleaning, time management, and problem-solving to maintain a stable and fulfilling lifestyle. Independent living allows individuals to exercise autonomy, self-reliance, and freedom in pursuing their goals and aspirations, while also promoting personal growth, confidence, and self-sufficiency.

pieces.name: Iran During World War II
pieces.about:
During World War II, Iran maintained its official neutrality, but it was strategically significant due to its location between the Allied powers (particularly the Soviet Union) and the Axis powers (especially Nazi Germany). In 1941, following a British-Soviet invasion known as the Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran, Iran's monarch, Reza Shah Pahlavi, was forced to abdicate in favor of his son, Mohammad Reza Shah.

The invasion was prompted by fears that Iran might align itself with Germany and provide a route for German forces to access oil fields in the Persian Gulf. The Allies also sought to secure Iranian transportation routes for the delivery of supplies to the Soviet Union.

During the war, Iran experienced significant economic and political upheaval. The Allied powers established a presence in the country, with British and Soviet troops stationed there. The Allies also pressured Iran to expel German nationals and enforce restrictions on German trade.

Overall, Iran's experience during World War II was marked by foreign intervention, internal political changes, and economic disruptions, setting the stage for further developments in the post-war period.

pieces.name: Islamic Art
pieces.about: Islamic art refers to the artistic traditions and expressions that have developed within the cultural and religious context of Islam. It encompasses a wide range of artistic forms, including architecture, calligraphy, painting, ceramics, textiles, and metalwork, among others. Islamic art is characterized by its emphasis on geometric patterns, arabesques, floral motifs, and intricate designs, often inspired by nature and religious symbolism. Calligraphy, particularly of Quranic verses, holds a central place in Islamic art, serving as a visual representation of Islamic beliefs and values. Islamic art is diverse and reflects the cultural influences of various regions and periods, from Spain to Southeast Asia, while also maintaining a distinct Islamic aesthetic and identity. (Page 293)

pieces.name: Isolation
pieces.about: Isolation refers to the state of being separated, detached, or cut off from others, either physically or socially. It can occur voluntarily or involuntarily and may have various causes and consequences, affecting individuals, communities, or societies in different ways.

pieces.name: Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
pieces.about: The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is a protracted and multifaceted dispute primarily centered around the territory of Israel, the Gaza Strip, and the West Bank. At its core, the conflict revolves around competing claims to land, historical narratives, and national aspirations.

pieces.name: Leaving Homeland
pieces.about: Leaving homeland refers to the act of departing or emigrating from one's native country or homeland to relocate to another region or country. This decision is often influenced by various factors, including economic opportunities, political instability, persecution, conflict, or personal circumstances. Leaving one's homeland can be a deeply significant and often difficult choice, involving the uprooting of one's life, family, and cultural ties in search of a better future or refuge from adversity. It can lead to a range of experiences and challenges, including cultural adjustment, homesickness, and the pursuit of new opportunities and aspirations in a foreign land.

pieces.name: Leninism
pieces.about: Leninism is a political theory and practice developed by Vladimir Lenin, the leader of the Bolshevik Party and the architect of the Russian Revolution of 1917. It represents an adaptation of Marxist principles to the conditions of Russia and other countries, emphasizing the need for a vanguard party to lead the proletariat in overthrowing capitalism and establishing socialism.

pieces.name: Living Abroad
pieces.about: Independent life in a foreign land refers to the experience of living autonomously in a country other than one's own, without relying on the support or assistance of family or friends from one's home country. It involves navigating unfamiliar cultural, social, and logistical challenges while managing daily responsibilities such as housing, finances, employment, and personal relationships. Independent life in a foreign land requires adaptability, resilience, and self-reliance, as individuals must learn to navigate new customs, languages, and social norms while building a support network and establishing a sense of belonging in their new environment. It offers opportunities for personal growth, cultural enrichment, and new experiences, but it can also involve loneliness, homesickness, and the need to overcome barriers to integration and success in a foreign culture.

pieces.name: Marriage Customs (Iran)
pieces.about:
Iranian marriage customs are deeply rooted in tradition, family values, and cultural practices that have evolved over centuries. While there may be variations across different regions and communities within Iran, some common customs and traditions include:

Arranged Marriages: Historically, arranged marriages were common in Iran, where families played a significant role in selecting a suitable partner for their children. While arranged marriages are still prevalent in some rural and traditional communities, urban Iranians increasingly participate in more modern forms of matchmaking and courtship.
Engagement (Khastegari): The process of marriage typically begins with khastegari, where the families of the prospective bride and groom meet to discuss the possibility of marriage. This informal gathering allows the families to get to know each other and determine compatibility.
Dowry (Mahr): In Iranian culture, the groom is traditionally expected to provide a mahr, or dowry, to the bride as a sign of his commitment and financial support. The mahr can include money, jewelry, property, or other valuable assets agreed upon by the families.
Wedding Ceremony (Aghd): The aghd, or wedding ceremony, is a formal and elaborate event that marks the union of the bride and groom. It typically involves rituals, customs, and traditions dating back centuries. During the ceremony, the couple exchanges vows, rings, and symbolic items, while family members and guests offer blessings and well-wishes.
Celebrations and Festivities: Iranian weddings are joyous occasions filled with music, dancing, feasting, and elaborate decorations. The celebrations can last for several days and often include traditional Persian rituals, such as the sofreh-ye aghd (wedding spread) and the knife dance (raghs-e chaghoo).
Family and Community Involvement: Marriage is not just a union between two individuals but also between their families and communities. Iranian weddings are often community affairs, with extended family members, friends, and neighbors coming together to celebrate the couple's union and offer support.
While modernization and changing social norms have influenced Iranian marriage customs to some extent, many traditional practices and values continue to play a significant role in shaping marital relationships and family life in Iran.

pieces.name: Marxism

pieces.name: Modern Imperialism (Iran)
pieces.about:
Modern imperialism in Iran refers to the influence and intervention of foreign powers in Iran's political, economic, and cultural affairs, particularly in the 20th and 21st centuries. One of the most notable examples of modern imperialism in Iran occurred with the Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran in 1941 during World War II. This invasion aimed to secure Iranian oil fields and transportation routes, as well as prevent Iran from aligning with Nazi Germany.

After World War II, Iran experienced further imperialistic actions, notably the overthrow of Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh in 1953 in a coup orchestrated by British and American intelligence agencies, with the support of the Shah of Iran. Mossadegh's government had nationalized Iran's oil industry, threatening Western interests. The coup restored Western-friendly leadership and reinstated British control over Iran's oil.

Throughout the Cold War, Iran became a key battleground for influence between the United States and the Soviet Union. The United States supported the autocratic rule of Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, who maintained close ties with the West and implemented modernization programs. However, this support led to resentment among Iranians and contributed to the 1979 Iranian Revolution, which resulted in the overthrow of the Shah and the establishment of an Islamic Republic.

pieces.name: National Exams
pieces.about: National exams are standardized assessments administered by a government or educational authority to measure the academic achievement, proficiency, or aptitude of students at a national level. These exams typically cover core subjects such as mathematics, language arts, science, and social studies, and may be conducted at various stages of a student's educational journey, such as the end of primary or secondary school. National exams serve several purposes, including assessing students' knowledge and skills, evaluating the effectiveness of educational programs and curricula, ranking schools or districts, and informing policy decisions related to education. Results from national exams may also be used for college admissions, scholarships, or other educational opportunities.

pieces.name: Nationalism
pieces.about: Nationalism is an ideology or movement that emphasizes the identity, unity, and interests of a particular nation or ethnic group. It promotes a strong sense of loyalty, pride, and attachment to one's nation, often prioritizing its sovereignty, culture, language, and history. Nationalism can manifest in various forms, including cultural nationalism, which emphasizes shared cultural heritage and traditions, and political nationalism, which seeks to assert or maintain national sovereignty and independence. While nationalism can foster solidarity and cohesion within a nation, it can also lead to exclusionary attitudes, ethnocentrism, and conflicts with other nations or ethnic groups.

pieces.name: Nationalization of Iran's Oil Industry
pieces.about:
The nationalization of Iran's oil industry occurred in 1951 when Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh's government passed legislation to nationalize the country's oil industry, which had been under British control through the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC), later known as British Petroleum (BP). Mossadegh's government argued that Iran should have more control over its own natural resources and sought to renegotiate the terms of the oil concession with the AIOC.

This move was met with strong opposition from Britain, which heavily relied on Iranian oil. In response, Britain imposed an embargo on Iranian oil exports and launched covert operations to undermine Mossadegh's government. The crisis came to a head in 1953 when Mossadegh was ousted in a coup orchestrated by British and American intelligence agencies, with the support of the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

Following the coup, the Shah regained power and reinstated British control over Iran's oil industry. The nationalization movement marked a significant moment in Iranian history, symbolizing the country's struggle for independence and sovereignty over its natural resources. However, the coup and its aftermath led to decades of authoritarian rule under the Shah, which ultimately contributed to the Iranian Revolution in 1979.

pieces.name: Nazism
pieces.about: Nazism refers to the ideology, policies, and practices associated with the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), commonly known as the Nazi Party, led by Adolf Hitler in Germany during the 1920s through the 1940s. Nazism is characterized by extreme nationalism, authoritarianism, racism, and anti-Semitism. It promoted the idea of a racially superior "Aryan" master race and sought to establish a totalitarian regime under Hitler's leadership. Nazism led to the systematic persecution, discrimination, and ultimately, genocide of millions of Jews, as well as other minority groups, during the Holocaust. The ideology of Nazism also encompassed expansionist and militaristic goals, leading to World War II and widespread devastation across Europe.

pieces.name: Parental Support
pieces.about: Parental support refers to the emotional, practical, and financial assistance provided by parents to their children throughout various stages of life. It encompasses a wide range of actions and behaviors aimed at nurturing, protecting, and promoting the well-being and development of children. Parental support can include offering love, encouragement, and guidance, providing basic needs such as food, shelter, and clothing, offering assistance with homework or school projects, attending important events or activities, and serving as a source of stability and security in times of crisis or uncertainty. Parental support plays a crucial role in fostering healthy relationships, self-esteem, and resilience in children, helping them navigate challenges, achieve their goals, and thrive in life.

pieces.name: Perspective
pieces.about: Perspective refers to a particular point of view or way of seeing and understanding the world, events, situations, or issues. It encompasses an individual's beliefs, attitudes, experiences, and biases, which shape their interpretation and understanding of reality. Perspective influences how people perceive and interpret information, make judgments, and form opinions about the world around them. It can vary among individuals based on factors such as cultural background, education, personal values, and life experiences. Understanding different perspectives is essential for empathy, effective communication, and collaboration in diverse social and cultural contexts.

pieces.name: Pride
pieces.about: Pride is a feeling of satisfaction, self-worth, or gratification derived from one's achievements, qualities, or possessions. It can also refer to a sense of dignity, self-respect, or confidence in one's abilities and identity. Pride often arises from a positive evaluation of oneself or one's accomplishments, leading to a sense of fulfillment, empowerment, and happiness. While pride can be a healthy and motivating emotion, excessive pride or arrogance may lead to hubris, overconfidence, and disregard for others.

pieces.name: Prison
pieces.about: Prison is a secure facility designed for the incarceration and confinement of individuals who have been convicted of committing crimes or who are awaiting trial. It is a form of punishment and rehabilitation used within the criminal justice system to restrict the freedom and movement of offenders as a means of protecting society, deterring crime, and promoting accountability and rehabilitation. Prisons typically house inmates in cells or dormitory-style accommodations and provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and medical care, as well as programs and services aimed at addressing behavioral issues, education, job training, and reintegration into society.

pieces.name: Psychoanalysis
pieces.about: Psychoanalysis is a psychological theory and therapeutic practice developed by Sigmund Freud that aims to explore and understand the unconscious mind, motivations, and conflicts that influence human behavior. It emphasizes the role of unconscious thoughts, desires, and early childhood experiences in shaping personality and psychological functioning. Through techniques such as free association, dream analysis, and transference, psychoanalysis seeks to uncover repressed memories and unconscious processes, leading to insight, resolution of inner conflicts, and psychological healing.

pieces.name: Public vs. Private Life
pieces.about:
Public life refers to activities, interactions, and affairs that occur within the public sphere and are accessible or observable by the broader community or society. This includes actions and behaviors conducted in public spaces, such as work, politics, social events, and community engagement. Public life often involves interactions with others and may be subject to scrutiny, accountability, and regulation by public institutions and authorities.

Private life, on the other hand, pertains to personal, intimate, and confidential matters that occur within the realm of one's personal space, relationships, and privacy. This includes activities and experiences conducted in private spaces, such as the home, family life, personal relationships, and individual thoughts and feelings. Private life is characterized by a degree of autonomy, confidentiality, and freedom from external interference or observation.

The distinction between public and private life is important for understanding the boundaries between personal autonomy and social responsibility, as well as the rights and expectations of individuals within society. While public life may involve participation in public discourse and engagement with the broader community, private life encompasses the sphere of personal autonomy, privacy, and individual rights.

pieces.name: Punk
pieces.about: Punk is a subculture and musical genre that emerged in the mid-1970s, primarily in the United States and the United Kingdom. Characterized by its DIY ethos, anti-establishment attitude, and raw, energetic music, punk became a platform for youth rebellion and social critique.

pieces.about: Treating people unfairly, or believing they are lesser, because of their race, and the ways this shows up in laws, institutions and everyday life.
